strengths: The paper addresses a practical problem: adapting quantized models to heterogeneous memory budgets without separately fine-tuning an adapter for every configuration.
Generating compact r×r transformations of configuration-specific SVD factors is a plausible, parameter-efficient design that avoids predicting entire LoRA adapters.

The evaluation covers four GLUE tasks, multiple generative models up to LLaMA-2-13B, different ranks, and integer quantization. Reported results show competitive perplexity and several accuracy improvements, with useful ablations of configuration search and Pareto segmentation.
weaknesses: The core search algorithm is insufficiently specified and contains consequential inconsistencies. Equation (6) maximizes expected hypervolume improvement, whereas Equation (8) and Algorithm 1 step in the negative-gradient direction. Perturbations of learned embeddings are not connected to a defined procedure for obtaining valid categorical configurations. The algorithm also does not specify how the GP is updated as candidates and adapter parameters change. These issues prevent verification of the central optimization procedure.

The comparisons do not adequately isolate the configuration-aware mapper's contribution. CoA-LoRA receives task-guided configuration search and configuration-specific SVD factors, while baselines use configurations obtained through Equation (11). Matched-configuration comparisons, an SVD-only control, and a shared r×r transformation using the same SVD factors would help distinguish gains from conditioning, initialization, and configuration selection.

Hypervolume comparisons are confounded by unequal configuration coverage: CoA-LoRA is evaluated on 50 configurations, while separately trained baselines receive five listed budgets or six solutions in Table 2. Denser sampling can improve hypervolume without improving performance at matched budgets. Appendix B also leaves bit-width normalization unclear despite specifying a (1,1) reference point.

The evidence does not establish adaptation to arbitrary configurations. Appendix A.3 explicitly selects new configurations for proximity to the optimized training set, supporting local interpolation. The evaluation does not adequately characterize configuration distances, held-out layer-level choices, or performance on substantially different allocations. This matters because the mapper conditions on each layer independently and cannot directly account for other layers' quantization settings.

The real-time and 'no additional time cost' claims exceed the measurements. Section 4.2 requires configuration-specific residual SVDs using full-precision weights. Their latency, storage or caching requirements, and preprocessing costs are not established. Table 2 reports RoBERTa training times, but there are no end-to-end adaptation measurements or device-level memory and latency results supporting the deployment claims.

Central numerical results require reconciliation. With rank 64 specified as the default, Table 2 reports a +8.89% MNLI accuracy gap over QLoRA, whereas Table 3 reports -0.63% at rank 64; QQP similarly changes from +7.87% to +0.67%. No protocol differences or uncertainty estimates explain these discrepancies, weakening confidence in the headline improvements.

Reproducibility is incomplete: hardware, batch sizes, C4 training volume, evaluation sample counts, repeated-run variability, and important search settings are missing. The implementation-availability sentence is unfinished and provides no usable link. Together with the methodological and reporting issues, these omissions leave the main claims insufficiently supported for acceptance.

Generating compact r×r adjustments within configuration-specific SVD bases is a sensible design that substantially reduces the hypernetwork’s output dimensionality.

The experiments cover four GLUE tasks, C4 perplexity, models up to LLaMA-2-13B, downstream zero-shot evaluation, and several ablations. Reported results are encouraging; for example, Table C.4 shows performance close to individually trained QLoRA at 3–4 bits.

Generation latency, SVD and search costs, caching requirements, and deployment memory are not measured comprehensively. The fixed-bit accuracy gaps are useful, but hypervolume gains require a common evaluation grid and fully specified normalization.
